clinicalPearls: Abnormal uterine bleeding describes any bleeding that is abnormal in frequency, regularity, duration, or volume in a non-pregnant woman of reproductive age

The FIGO PALM-COEIN system classifies causes into structural (polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy and hyperplasia) and non-structural (coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic, not otherwise classified) categories
Excluding pregnancy is the essential first step in any woman of reproductive age presenting with abnormal bleeding
Ovulatory dysfunction, common at the extremes of reproductive life, produces irregular unpredictable bleeding from unopposed oestrogen effect on the endometrium
An underlying bleeding disorder, particularly von Willebrand disease, should be considered in women with heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche

Endometrial sampling is indicated in women at risk of hyperplasia or malignancy, such as those over a threshold age, with persistent bleeding, or with risk factors like obesity and chronic anovulation
Medical management includes hormonal options and antifibrinolytic and anti-inflammatory agents, with the levonorgestrel intrauterine system being highly effective for heavy menstrual bleeding
Surgical options such as endometrial ablation or hysterectomy are reserved for failed medical therapy or specific structural causes
reference.pathophysiology: Normal menstruation depends on cyclical ovulation producing coordinated oestrogen and progesterone effects, followed by orderly progesterone withdrawal and controlled endometrial shedding with effective local haemostasis. Abnormal bleeding arises when this is disrupted: structural lesions (polyps, adenomyosis, fibroids, hyperplasia or cancer) distort the endometrium and its vasculature; anovulation leads to unopposed oestrogen with an unstable proliferative endometrium that sheds erratically; systemic coagulopathy impairs haemostasis; and local disturbances of endometrial prostaglandins and fibrinolysis increase menstrual loss.
additionalDifferentials: Pregnancy-related bleeding including miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy
Cervical or vaginal lesions including malignancy
additionalInvestigations: Pregnancy test in women of reproductive age
Full blood count to assess for iron-deficiency anaemia
Transvaginal ultrasound to assess endometrial thickness and detect structural lesions
Endometrial biopsy or hysteroscopy with directed sampling where malignancy or hyperplasia is a concern
Coagulation screen and von Willebrand testing when a bleeding disorder is suspected
Thyroid function tests and other endocrine investigations as indicated
redFlags: Postmenopausal bleeding, which must be investigated to exclude endometrial carcinoma
Heavy bleeding causing haemodynamic instability or severe symptomatic anaemia
Bleeding with risk factors for endometrial cancer such as obesity, chronic anovulation, or tamoxifen use
A suspicious cervical or vaginal lesion on examination
Intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding suggesting cervical pathology
reference.prognosis: Most abnormal uterine bleeding is benign and responds well to medical or targeted surgical treatment, with good symptom control and correction of anaemia. Prognosis in structural or malignant causes depends on the underlying diagnosis, so timely investigation to identify hyperplasia or carcinoma is key to a favourable outcome.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude pregnancy before investigation or treatment
Attributing postmenopausal bleeding to benign causes without excluding malignancy
Overlooking an inherited bleeding disorder in a young woman with lifelong heavy periods
Not sampling the endometrium in women with risk factors for hyperplasia or cancer
Treating presumed dysfunctional bleeding without excluding structural lesions
